mcq.question: As per Section 16(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, a registered person is entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him subject to certain conditions. Which of the following is a fundamental condition regarding the use of such goods or services for claiming Input Tax Credit (ITC)?

options.label: A
options.text: The registered person must have actually paid the tax charged on the supply to the supplier before claiming the credit.
options.explanation: This incorrectly conflates the condition of possession of invoice and receipt of goods with payment of tax to the supplier. Under Section 16(2), the conditions relate to possession of invoice, receipt of goods, and the supplier having furnished the return. Payment to the supplier is not a statutory condition for ITC eligibility under Section 16.

options.label: B
options.text: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business.
options.explanation: Section 16(1) explicitly mandates that ITC is available only on goods or services which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of the business. This establishes the direct nexus between the input and business activity required for credit eligibility.

options.label: C
options.text: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used for personal consumption of the registered person.
options.explanation: This is the direct opposite of the requirement under Section 16(1). The statute explicitly requires goods/services to be used 'in the course or furtherance of his business'. Use for personal consumption is a non-business purpose, and Section 17(5) specifically blocks ITC on goods/services used for personal consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used exclusively for the manufacture of capital goods.
options.explanation: This incorrectly narrows the scope of ITC eligibility. Section 16(1) permits ITC for goods/services used 'in the course or furtherance of his business', which is a broad requirement covering all business activities including trading, services, and manufacturing. The statute does not require exclusive use for manufacture of capital goods.

mcq.explanation: Section 16(1) states that every registered person shall be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business. If goods are diverted for non-business purposes, the registered person is not entitled to ITC on such goods.

mcq.question: Mr. A, a registered person, is in possession of a tax invoice for a supply of goods. However, the details of the said invoice have not been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies. Can Mr. A avail the Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the basis of the tax invoice in his possession?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because possession of a valid tax invoice is the primary condition for availing Input Tax Credit under Section 16(2)(a).
options.explanation: This incorrectly assumes that satisfying one condition (possession of invoice under Section 16(2)(a)) is sufficient. Section 16(2) uses 'and' to connect the conditions; the invoice details must also be furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies under Section 16(2)(aa).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because the recipient can claim ITC based on the invoice if the tax has been charged and the goods have been received.
options.explanation: This overlooks the mandatory requirement introduced by Section 16(2)(aa). Even if goods are received and tax is charged, ITC cannot be availed unless the supplier has furnished the invoice details in the statement of outward supplies and these have been communicated to the recipient.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because the recipient has not actually paid the tax amount to the supplier against the said invoice.
options.explanation: This gives the right answer (No) but for the wrong reason. Payment of tax to the supplier is not a condition for ITC under Section 16. The correct reason for denial is the failure to satisfy Section 16(2)(aa) regarding furnishing of invoice details in the statement of outward supplies.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because the details of the invoice have not been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and communicated to the recipient.
options.explanation: Section 16(2)(aa) mandates that the details of the invoice or debit note must be furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and communicated to the recipient. Mere possession of the tax invoice is insufficient if this condition is not met.

mcq.explanation: As per Section 16(2), a registered person is not entitled to credit of any input tax unless the details of the invoice have been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and such details have been communicated to the recipient in the manner specified under section 37. This condition is in addition to possessing a valid tax invoice under Section 16(2)(a).

mcq.question: M/s Alpha Ltd., a manufacturing company, availed works contract services for renovation of its factory building. The expenditure for such renovation was not capitalized in the books of account but was treated as revenue expenditure in accordance with the applicable Accounting Standards. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the admissibility of Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the GST paid for such works contract services?

options.label: A
options.text: ITC is blocked because the factory building is an immovable property other than plant and machinery.
options.explanation: While the factory building is indeed an immovable property other than plant and machinery, the candidate fails to apply the specific exception for non-capitalized renovation/repairs. The blocking of ITC under Section 17(5)(c) applies only when the construction (including renovation) is capitalized.

options.label: B
options.text: ITC is allowed since the renovation expenditure is not capitalized in the books of account.
options.explanation: As per the definition of 'construction' in the context of blocked credits, renovation amounts to construction only if it is capitalized. Since the expense is treated as revenue expenditure (not capitalized), it does not fall within the blocked credit provisions of section 17(5)(c).

options.label: C
options.text: ITC is blocked because renovation of a factory building amounts to construction of an immovable property other than plant and machinery.
options.explanation: This option incorrectly applies the blocking provision by ignoring the vital qualification regarding capitalization. The definition of 'construction' explicitly includes renovation only 'to the extent of capitalization'. Since the facts state the expenditure was not capitalized, it does not amount to 'construction' for the purpose of Section 17(5)(c), and thus ITC is not blocked.

options.label: D
options.text: ITC is allowed only if M/s Alpha Ltd. is in the business of providing works contract services to others.
options.explanation: This incorrectly applies the restriction for works contract services used for further supply of works contract services (sub-contracting). The reference material clarifies that when renovation/repairs are not capitalized, ITC is allowed to 'all the recipients irrespective of their line of business'.

mcq.explanation: Section 17(5)(c) blocks ITC on works contract services supplied for construction of an immovable property, other than plant and machinery. The term 'construction' explicitly includes re-construction, renovation, additions or alterations, or repairs, but only 'to the extent of capitalization' to the said immovable property. The reference material states that if renovation or repairs are not capitalized, it would not tantamount to construction under GST law. Consequently, ITC on works contract services availed for such construction (which is not capitalized) is allowed to all recipients irrespective of their line of business. mcq.question: Delta Traders, a registered person, had its registration cancelled with effect from 1st August 2025. The cancellation order was subsequently revoked on 20th October 2026. Delta Traders filed all pending returns for the period from the cancellation date to the revocation date on 15th November 2026 (within 30 days of revocation). Delta Traders possesses an invoice dated 1st May 2025 (pertaining to FY 2025-26) for which ITC was not availed before cancellation. Determine the last date for Delta Traders to avail ITC on the invoice dated 1st May 2025.

mcq.explanation: Section 16(6) provides a specific relaxation for cases where registration is cancelled and subsequently revoked. If the taxpayer files the returns for the period from cancellation to revocation within 30 days of the revocation order, the time limit to avail ITC under Section 16(4) is extended to the date of filing of those returns. However, this extension is subject to the condition that the time limit under Section 16(4) had not already expired on the date of cancellation. In this scenario, the invoice is dated 1st May 2025. The normal deadline under Section 16(4) would be 30th November 2026. The registration was cancelled on 1st August 2025. On the date of cancellation, the Section 16(4) deadline (30th November 2026) had not expired. Therefore, the relaxation applies. Since the returns were filed on 15th November 2026, this becomes the last date to avail the ITC.

The extended deadline under Section 16(6) is the date of filing of the return for the gap period, which is 15th November 2026. But the relaxation allows availing ITC until 30th November 2026, as the original deadline was still valid at cancellation. Hence, the last date is 30th November 2026. mcq.question: Which of the following statements regarding the methodology for determination of input tax credit on capital goods under Rule 43 are correct? (select all that apply)

options.label: A
options.text: The useful life of capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall be taken as five years from the date of the invoice for such goods.
options.explanation: The five-year useful life rule applies only to common capital goods used for both taxable and exempt supplies (covered under clause (c) of Rule 43). For capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies, the credit itself is not allowed to be credited to the electronic credit ledger, so the question of useful life for reversal does not arise.

options.label: B
options.text: The amount of input tax on capital goods used exclusively for effecting taxable supplies including zero-rated supplies shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger.
options.explanation: Rule 43(1)(b) provides that input tax on capital goods used exclusively for taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger.

options.label: C
options.text: The amount of input tax on capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall not be credited to the electronic credit ledger.
options.explanation: Rule 43(1)(a) specifies that input tax on capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall not be credited to the electronic credit ledger.

options.label: D
options.text: The useful life of capital goods used for both taxable and exempt supplies is taken as five years from the date of the invoice for such goods.
options.explanation: Rule 43(1)(c) explicitly states that the useful life of capital goods (not covered under exclusive use) shall be taken as five years from the date of the invoice.

mcq.explanation: Rule 43 prescribes the manner of determining ITC on capital goods. It mandates that credit for capital goods used exclusively for non-business or exempt purposes is blocked. For capital goods used exclusively for taxable supplies, full credit is allowed. For common capital goods (used for both taxable and exempt supplies), the credit is credited to the ledger and the useful life is deemed to be five years for the purpose of reversal calculations.

mcq.question: Satyamev Printers undertakes the printing of books where the content is supplied by the publisher, but the physical inputs including paper belong to the printer. The supply is billed at a single price. What is the nature and tax treatment of this supply?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of goods, being the principal supply.
options.explanation: While the candidate correctly identifies the transaction as a composite supply, they misidentify the principal supply. The material clarifies that when physical inputs belong to the printer, the supply of printing is the principal supply (a service), not the goods.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a mixed supply and shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax.
options.explanation: The candidate confuses composite supply with mixed supply. Printing of books with physical inputs from the printer is naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business, making it a composite supply, not a mixed supply.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of goods since the printed books are physically delivered to the publisher.
options.explanation: The candidate focuses on the physical delivery of goods (books) rather than the statutory condition that determines the principal supply. The material specifies that where physical inputs belong to the printer, printing is the principal supply (service).

options.label: D
options.text: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of services, being the principal supply.
options.explanation: As per the reference material, the supply of printed books where physical inputs belong to the printer is a composite supply. The principal supply is the supply of printing services, and thus the entire supply is treated as a supply of services.

mcq.explanation: The supply described is a composite supply because it comprises two or more supplies (printing service and goods like paper) naturally bundled in conjunction with each other. According to the analysis in the material, for the printing of books where physical inputs belong to the printer, the principal supply is the supply of printing services. Under Section 8(a), a composite supply is treated as a supply of its principal supply. Therefore, the transaction is treated as a supply of services chargeable to the rate applicable to printing services.

evidence.quote: The above circular further clarifies that in the composite supply of printing of books, pamphlets, brochures, annual reports, and the like, where only content is supplied by the publisher or the person who owns the usage rights to the intangible inputs while the physical inputs including paper used for printing belong to the printer, supply of printing [of the content supplied by the recipient of supply] is the principal supply and therefore such supplies would constitute supply of service.
Accordingly, in the given case, the supply of printed books by Satyamev Printers is a composite supply wherein the principal supply is supply of printing services.

options.label: D

mcq.question: Mr. Chakmak, a proprietor registered in Delhi, received architectural services without consideration from his son located in the US. Which of the following statements correctly determines the taxability of this transaction under the GST law?

options.label: A
options.text: It will not qualify as supply in either case, since services received without consideration from a related person can never be treated as supply under the GST law.
options.explanation: This incorrectly assumes that absence of consideration automatically exempts the transaction. Under Entry 4 of Schedule I, import of services without consideration from a related person IS treated as supply if received in the course or furtherance of business.

options.label: B
options.text: It will qualify as supply in both cases, since import of services by a related person without consideration is treated as supply irrespective of whether it is in the course or furtherance of business.
options.explanation: This confuses the rule for import of services WITH consideration (which is supply regardless of business purpose) with import WITHOUT consideration (which requires the 'in course or furtherance of business' condition).

options.label: C
options.text: It will not qualify as supply if the services are received with respect to his newly constructed house, but will qualify as supply if received with respect to his office in Delhi.
options.explanation: As per the provisions of Schedule I read with section 7(1)(c), import of services by a person from a related person without consideration is treated as supply only if it is in the course or furtherance of business. Services for a personal house are not in the course of business, whereas services for an office are.

options.label: B
options.text: Jaipur, Rajasthan
options.explanation: Under Section 12(2)(b)(i) of the IGST Act, for services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location of the recipient where the address on record exists. Since the address of M/s Global Traders on record is in Jaipur, Rajasthan, that is the place of supply, regardless of where the goods are transported or where the service is effectively used.

options.text: Mumbai, Maharashtra
options.explanation: The candidate may misapply the default provision under Section 12(2)(b) by concluding that since the recipient is unregistered, the 'other cases' clause (location of supplier) applies. options.text: Delhi
options.explanation: The candidate may incorrectly rely on the origin and destination of the goods transported (Delhi to Chennai) to determine the place of supply. mcq.explanation:
The place of supply of services where both the supplier and recipient are in India is governed by Section 12 of the IGST Act. Section 12 does not contain a specific provision for the transportation of goods (unlike Section 12(8) for passenger transport or specific clauses for other services). Therefore, the default provision under Section 12(2) applies. 

Section 12(2)(b) provides that for services made to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location of the recipient where the address on record exists, and the location of the supplier in other cases. The Study Material explicitly states that for unregistered persons, the place of supply is the location of such unregistered person if the address is available in the records of the supplier. The fact that the service is effectively used in Chennai or that the goods moved from Delhi to Chennai is irrelevant for the default rule. The statutory requirement is satisfied by the 'address on record', which is Jaipur. The Study Material emphasizes that the provisions of Section 12 are in relation to domestic supply and the default rule relies on the address available in the records.

option_verdicts.label: A
option_verdicts.comment: Although the statutory default under Section 12(2)(b)(i) points to the address on record (Jaipur), the recipient is unregistered and has no actual presence in Rajasthan. The service is effectively used in Chennai by its branch, raising a plausible argument under principles of 'effective use' or business reality. While the Study Material does not extend Section 13(13)-like logic to domestic supplies, a well-prepared candidate could argue that reliance on a 'nominal' address disconnected from actual operations leads to an artificial result, especially when the recipient lacks nexus with Jaipur. This makes the option arguable, though not strictly correct under current law.

option_verdicts.label: B
option_verdicts.comment: This aligns with Section 12(2)(b)(i) and the Study Material (C3, C5), which state that for services to unregistered persons, if an address on record exists, the place of supply is the location of the recipient based on that address. The fact that the address is in Jaipur and on record satisfies the statutory condition. The explanation correctly emphasizes that actual use or operational presence is irrelevant under the default rule.

option_verdicts.label: C
option_verdicts.comment: Option C (Mumbai) would only apply if no address on record existed for the unregistered recipient (per Section 12(2)(b)(ii)). Since an address (Jaipur) is on record, this fallback does not apply. A candidate might misread the hierarchy of rules, but the distractor is moderately tempting only if they misunderstand the conditional structure of Section 12(2)(b).

option_verdicts.label: D
option_verdicts.comment: Delhi is merely the origin of goods; there is no provision in Section 12 linking place of supply to origin or destination of transported goods. This option is weak and unlikely to tempt a well-prepared candidate unless they are guessing based on movement of goods rather than recipient location.

issues.detail: The term 'address on record' is used without defining whether it must reflect a genuine business connection or can be a nominal/billing address with no operational nexus. The scenario states the recipient has no presence or operations in Rajasthan, making the Jaipur address effectively a paper address. The Study Material (C5) states the rule depends on 'availability' of address in records, not its authenticity or operational relevance. However, this creates ambiguity: does 'on record' include addresses known by the supplier to be non-functional or fictitious? If so, the law may be applied mechanically, but candidates may reasonably question whether such an address constitutes a valid 'location of the recipient' under the Act.

Option A (Chennai) is arguable due to the effective use and operational reality, even though the official rule favors B. While the Study Material does not recognize 'effective use' for domestic supplies under Section 12, it acknowledges such a principle in cross-border cases under Section 13(13). A strong candidate could argue that applying a purely documentary rule (Jaipur) when the recipient has no nexus there and the service is fully consumed in Chennai leads to an anomalous result. Given that the recipient’s 'location' should reflect economic reality, and considering judicial trends favoring substance over form, two answers (A and B) are defensible, undermining the single-correct format.

The explanation states that Section 12 does not contain a specific provision for transportation of goods. However, while there is no explicit clause for goods transport under Section 12(3)-(14), the absence of a specific rule reinforces the application of the default rule under Section 12(2), which is correctly applied. This part of the explanation is acceptable, though slightly imprecise. The real issue lies in not acknowledging that the lack of a specific rule makes the default rule the only guide, which increases reliance on 'address on record'—but this is not inconsistent per se.

examiner.summary: The question hinges on a technically correct application of Section 12(2)(b)(i), but the scenario creates a conflict between statutory form (address on record) and economic substance (actual use in Chennai). While Option B is legally correct per the Study Material, Option A is sufficiently arguable due to the recipient's lack of nexus with Jaipur, making two answers defensible. This undermines the single-correct format. The term 'address on record' is ambiguous without clarification on whether it must reflect a genuine business connection. The question must be revised to either strengthen the legitimacy of the Jaipur address or clarify that nominal addresses are sufficient under law.

mcq.question: M/s Eventz India, a registered entity in New Delhi, is engaged by M/s Tech Solutions, an unregistered person located in Gurugram, Haryana, to organize a 3-day business conference. The conference is scheduled to be held in Kathmandu, Nepal. M/s Eventz India raises the invoice for their services on 10th October, 2026. Determine the place of supply of the event organization services provided by M/s Eventz India.

options.label: A
options.text: Kathmandu, Nepal
options.explanation: The candidate may correctly recall the general rule that for event management services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is where the event is actually held, but fail to register the crucial exception stated in the proviso: if the event is held outside India, the place of supply shifts to the location of the recipient.

options.label: B
options.text: Gurugram, Haryana
options.explanation: As per Section 12(7)(a)(ii) of the IGST Act, for event organization services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location where the event is actually held. However, a proviso states that if the event is held outside India, the place of supply shall be the location of the recipient. Since the event is in Kathmandu (outside India) and the recipient is in Gurugram, the place of supply is Gurugram.

options.label: C
options.text: New Delhi
options.explanation: The candidate may ignore the specific provision for event management services (Section 12(7)) and apply the default provision (Section 12(2)) for unregistered persons incorrectly. Under the default rule for unregistered persons without an address on record, the place of supply would be the supplier's location (New Delhi), but this ignores the specific event management provision.

options.label: D
options.text: Bengaluru, Karnataka
options.explanation: The candidate may confuse the facts of the current question with the illustration provided in the Study Material (where Mr. Murthy's event was held in Bengaluru). This represents a failure to apply the legal provision to the specific facts of the case at hand, instead recalling the answer to a different illustrative example.

options.label: A
options.text: The recipient is required to reverse the proportionate ITC as the discount will be excluded from the value of supply upon issuance of credit note.
options.explanation: Under the amendment proposed by the Finance Act, 2026, once it comes into effect, the discount will be excluded from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. options.label: B

However, under the amended provisions, the discount will be excluded from the value of supply only if the recipient reverses the proportionate ITC.

options.label: C
options.text: The recipient is eligible to retain the ITC as the discount provided is in the nature of a post supply discount which does not affect the tax liability of the original transaction.
options.explanation: This incorrectly assumes that post supply discounts continue to have no impact on ITC retention. options.label: D
options.text: The recipient cannot claim any reduction in value of supply as the post supply discount agreement was not in existence at the time of the original supply and cannot be linked invoice-wise.
options.explanation: This statement applies the pre-amendment conditions which required the agreement to exist at the time of supply and be capable of being linked invoice-wise. The Finance Act, 2026 amendment specifically removes these conditions, making it unnecessary for the agreement to exist at the time of supply.
